newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Mexico's upstart TV Azteca going public.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mexico's upstart TV Azteca going public.

text.p: Mexican broadcaster TV Azteca on Monday said it planned to go public in the largest initial stock offering by a Mexican company since the country's devastating 1994-95 peso crisis.
Depending on market conditions, Azteca said it would place $600 million to $680 million of shares both in Mexico and on the New York Stock Exchange as American Depository Shares (ADSs).

The company did not say when it would launch the offer. It may wait until after the U.S. summer months when many investors are on holiday, or until Mexico looks safe from currency worries in Brazilian markets, analysts said.
The offer represents about a third of TV Azteca's total share capital, company officials said. Chairman Ricardo Salinas Pliego, who owns a controlling stake, is not selling any of his shares.

"The principal purpose of this offering is to provide liquidity to certain minority shareholders and to generate funds to be used by TV Azteca for general corporate purposes," the company said in a statement.

Having launched a challenge against Grupo Televisa on the airwaves, Azteca will now compete against its larger rival in stock markets as well. Televisa is currently the only listed Mexican television company.
"On a fundamental basis, there will not be an effect on Televisa because both companies are already competing," Marla Marron, an analyst at ING Barings, said.
In 1996, Azteca's weekday audience share during prime time grew from 18 percent in January to 37 percent by year's end, according to the company.

Azteca has wooed viewers by offering slick newscasts, racy soap operas and U.S.-style news tabloid shows such as "Ciudad Desnuda" ("Naked City"). That show, the broadcaster's most successful hourlong program, features segments on crime, adultery and the like.

The network began to rattle its monolithic rival Televisa in 1996 with its popular soap opera "Nada Personal." Although Televisa successfully exported Mexican soap operas for years, Azteca crafted a racy story that dealt with betrayal and corruption in Mexico's ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party -- previously taboo subjects that fascinated ordinary Mexicans.
Bear Stearns and Co will lead the offering of ADS's outside Mexico, while Banco Inbursa and Grupo Financiero Serfin are co-leading the offer in Mexico.
